identity.title: Senescence induces clonal failure of hepatocyte plasticity and reshapes regenerative lineages.

content.abstract: BACKGROUND & AIMS: Telomere dysregulation is a central driver of cellular senescence and chronic liver disease. Yet how physiological telomeric attrition, rather than uniform telomere loss, leads to hepatic functional decline remains unclear. We therefore investigate how resolvable telomere dysfunction reshapes liver regeneration. METHODS: An adeno-associated virus (AAV)-CRISPR-based strategy was developed to induce resolvable telomeric breaks in mouse hepatocytes while preserving endogenous telomere maintenance. Clonal dynamics, lineage tracing, and single-nucleus transcriptomic profiling were used to characterize senescent hepatocyte behavior during chronic liver injury. Human cirrhotic liver samples were analyzed to assess the relationship between hepatocyte telomere length and intermediate cellular states. An in vivo CRISPR screen identified regulators of hepatocyte plasticity under telomere stress. RESULTS: Telomere-induced senescence did not substantially impair hepatocyte survival or basal metabolic function, but induced a clonal imbalance shaped by telomerase expression. Lineage tracing and single-nucleus transcriptomics demonstrated that senescent hepatocytes exhibited impaired hepatocyte-to-ductal metaplasia during chronic injury, with limited entry into the dedifferentiated state and failure to fully activate the ductal program. This incomplete transition disrupted epithelial composition and exacerbated the ductular reaction. Analyses of human cirrhotic livers revealed an association between preserved telomere integrity and bipotent hepatocyte states. Furthermore, the in vivo CRISPR screen identified regulators of hepatocyte dedifferentiation under telomere stress. CONCLUSIONS: These findings identify senescence as a barrier to hepatobiliary clonal balance rather than a direct trigger of hepatocyte loss. Telomere dysfunction thereby promotes pathological epithelial remodeling during chronic liver injury. IMPACT AND IMPLICATIONS: Telomere shortening is a common feature of chronic liver disease, but how it functionally contributes to regenerative failure remains incompletely understood. Our study shows that telomere dysfunction does not simply compromise hepatocyte survival or basal metabolic capacity. Instead, senescence acts as a clonal and lineage-selective constraint that limits hepatocyte plasticity and alters which cells contribute to regeneration. These findings provide a mechanistic link between telomere attrition, loss of regenerative diversity, and progressive liver dysfunction, and suggest that preservation of hepatocyte plasticity may be an important determinant of regenerative capacity in chronic liver disease.
